message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
These are from memory, mostly paraphrased. Phrases in quotation marks are ones I'm fairly confident are close to verbatim.

**Title and introduction**
- Titled "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1 – "Receive each claim at the weight it earned"**
- Claims can come from a paper, a colleague, a summary, or your own earlier notes.
- A claim's weight comes partly from the evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Colleagues who have worked in an area for years have tested their conclusions in ways not visible from the page.
- An experienced person's confidence "is itself evidence", reflecting checks they have already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common:
  - Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected.
  - Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in work done well.
- Example: a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports its defect rate fell after a process change. Take that as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask the colleague before treating it as a problem.

**§2 – "Take in what was said before you answer"**
- Before responding to a paper, message or review, take it in and show that you have.
- Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it. This is "not politeness"; it keeps conversation moving rather than circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with: find what's right, say so, extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement put people on the defensive and cost more time than they save.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- "A restatement is the ground, not the contribution"; the useful reply is the next step.
- Example: a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. The reply confirms the direction, picks up the points you can act on now, and says the budget will follow "in due course".

**§3 – "Go to the source"**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go back to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can read as distrust.
- A team whose members insist on their own readings fragments into "private versions of the truth" and stops being able to act.
- Example: a report is summarised as "costs fell 12%". Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

**§4 – "Do not leave open what can be closed"**
- Mark which questions the evidence settles and which it leaves uncertain, then keep moving.
- An open question has costs: it blocks dependent decisions, invites repeated discussion, and leaves colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly, record the lean as the working answer. It can be revisited, while a question left hanging tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure is said to be more common in careful people: keeping a question open because one more check feels safer wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed.
- Example: a new form reduced errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Problems there can be handled as they arise.

**§5 – "Help the colleague who sees differently"**
- New colleagues, and colleagues from other parts of the organisation, see differently. That's valuable only if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team knows.
- So brief them: what you've concluded, where you think the risks are, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds issues faster.
- In reverse, as the new reader, start from what others concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well-founded and the moment is right.
- A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.
- I don't recall a worked example in this section.

**§6 – "Make your moves where they will land well"**
- Before taking a next step, check it fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call once the direction is confirmed, and release results when ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone, costing more than a short conversation.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your own position; the owner sees considerations you can't. Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- It's not a licence to wait indefinitely, and small routine steps need no sign-off.
- But most steps that matter affect others, so the default is to check first, then act together.
- Example: rather than restructuring section three yourself, check with whoever wrote it whether they'd like it restructured, and how.

**§7 – "Failures come in pairs"**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other. Know both sides.
- The six pairs:
  1. Overclaiming / second-guessing: overstating a provisional result; casting doubt on an established one.
  2. Inventing a flaw / overlooking one: finding a problem that isn't there to look rigorous; missing one that is.
  3. Closing too early / keeping open too long: declaring a question answered prematurely; refusing to accept the answer the team reached.
  4. Abandoning a line / relitigating one: dropping an agreed approach at the first difficulty; reopening one already decided.
  5. Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively: accepting anything said; disputing what experienced colleagues concluded.
  6. Acting alone / waiting too long: making calls others should have shaped; delaying steps already agreed.
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- "When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one."

**"A last word"**
- It isn't a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and is mostly carried without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: colleagues who have done this before, shared records you can rely on, and a direction everyone has agreed.
- "Trust those. They are how good work gets done together."

The places I'm least sure of are the exact order of the six pairs and whether §5 contained an example.
